segments.text: Social psychology studies how people’s thoughts, feelings and behaviour are influenced by other people and by social situations. This unit focuses on group influence, explanations of behaviour, helping, attitudes and social norms.
The best preparation method is concept + classic finding + everyday application + limitation. That prevents the answer from becoming a list of famous experiments.

items.text: Social facilitation
: The presence of others can change performance. Well-learned or simple responses may improve in some situations, while difficult or unfamiliar tasks may suffer under evaluation or arousal.
Attribution
: Attribution is the process of explaining why behaviour occurred. People may emphasize internal dispositions or external situations, and judgment can be biased when information is incomplete.
Conformity

: Conformity is changing behaviour or expressed belief in response to real or imagined group pressure. Normative influence concerns acceptance; informational influence concerns believing others may know better.
Obedience
: Obedience concerns responding to commands from an authority. It is distinct from conformity, although both involve social influence.
Altruism and helping
: Helping behaviour is influenced by empathy, perceived responsibility, costs and benefits, social norms and features of the situation. The bystander effect is an important application.
Attitudes
: Attitudes are evaluations of people, objects or issues. They can involve cognitive, affective and behavioural tendencies, and they may change through persuasion, experience or cognitive processes.
Social norms
: Norms are shared expectations about appropriate behaviour. They can guide behaviour even when no formal law exists.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

Social psychology shows that behaviour often changes with roles, norms, group membership and situational cues. This does not erase personality. A better model treats behaviour as an interaction between person and situation, with interpretation mediating how the situation is experienced.

items.text: Attribution

: People explain behaviour using internal causes such as traits and external causes such as constraints. The fundamental attribution error describes a tendency, especially documented in many Western samples, to underweight situational causes when explaining others. Cultural variation means it should not be written as a universal law.
Self-serving patterns
: People may explain successes and failures in ways that protect self-image, but the direction and strength of such biases vary across contexts and cultures.
Normative influence
: People may conform to gain acceptance or avoid rejection even when they privately disagree. Group unanimity and public responding can increase pressure.
Informational influence
: People may conform because they believe others possess useful information, especially in ambiguous situations. Here the group changes perceived reality, not merely public behaviour.
Asch studies

: Asch's line-judgment experiments showed that many participants sometimes conformed to an obviously incorrect majority, while substantial individual differences remained. The studies demonstrate conditional social pressure, not automatic obedience.
Obedience

: Milgram's studies examined compliance with authority instructions in a laboratory setting. The findings demonstrated that situational structure can powerfully influence behaviour, while later debate emphasized ethics, interpretation and historical context.
Conformity versus obedience
: Conformity usually involves pressure from peers or group norms; obedience involves a command from an authority. The processes can overlap but should not be used as synonyms.
Social facilitation
: The presence or evaluation of others can increase arousal and strengthen dominant responses. Well-practised responses may improve while difficult or unfamiliar tasks may worsen.
Social loafing
: When individual effort is less identifiable in group work, some people may reduce effort. Clear roles, accountability and meaningful group identity can reduce the problem.
Group polarization
: Discussion among like-minded members can shift the average position toward a more extreme version of the group's initial tendency. Information exchange and social comparison both contribute.
Groupthink

: Highly cohesive decision groups can suppress dissent and fail to examine alternatives, especially under pressure and directive leadership. The concept is useful but should not be treated as an inevitable feature of cohesive groups.
Bystander effect

: Research following the work of Latané and Darley showed that the presence of others can reduce intervention in some emergencies through diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance. The effect depends on context rather than occurring every time.
Decision sequence
: Helping requires noticing the event, interpreting it as requiring help, accepting responsibility, knowing or choosing a response and acting. Failure at any stage can prevent intervention.
Determinants of helping
: Empathy, relationship, perceived danger, norms, costs, competence and time pressure can affect helping. Prosocial behaviour therefore cannot be explained by one motive.
Attitude components
: Attitudes include evaluations and may involve beliefs, feelings and action tendencies. These components can be inconsistent, which is one reason attitudes do not always predict behaviour perfectly.
Persuasion

: Source credibility, message quality, audience involvement and emotional framing influence persuasion. Strongly held attitudes are usually more resistant to change than weak or newly formed attitudes.
Cognitive dissonance
: Dissonance theory proposes discomfort when behaviour and important beliefs conflict. People may reduce inconsistency by changing attitudes, changing behaviour or reinterpreting the situation.
Norms
: Descriptive norms communicate what people commonly do, while injunctive norms communicate what people approve or disapprove. Confusing the two can produce weak behaviour-change messages.

rows: Avoid this error Do not describe classic experiments as if every person reacts exactly the same way. They demonstrate tendencies under particular conditions, not fixed laws for every individual.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define social influence, explain facilitation and attribution, compare conformity and obedience, then cover helping, attitudes and norms with one application each.
• Asch (1956) on conformity; Milgram (1963) on obedience; Latané & Darley (1970) on bystander intervention.
• Social situations can strongly influence behaviour.
• Conformity is group pressure; obedience involves authority commands.
• Attributions can overemphasize personal traits and underweight situations.
• Norms guide behaviour through shared expectations.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
